Why Masters Week in Augusta Is Different From Any Other Trip

If you're planning a Masters Week trip to Augusta, the first thing to understand is that this is not a normal golf tournament week. Augusta National Golf Club sits on Washington Road, and for one week each April the entire city reorganizes around it. Hotel rates triple. Restaurant wait times stretch to two hours. Washington Road becomes a one-way crawl. Locals who can leave, leave.

The good news: with the right plan, Masters Week is one of the great American travel experiences. The bad news: most visitors plan it like a standard city trip and spend half their week stuck in traffic on Berckmans Road or paying $80 a night to park at a strip mall. This guide is the local version — where to stay, how to move around, what to eat, and how to actually enjoy the week instead of surviving it.

Step 1: Lock In Your Lodging First (Before Anything Else)

Masters Week lodging in Augusta sells out six to twelve months in advance. If you're reading this in January or later, you're already behind — but not out of options if you know where to look.

Here's the honest hierarchy of Masters Week accommodations:

  • Downtown Augusta hotels: Convenient to the Riverwalk and Broad Street restaurants, but parking is a nightmare during tournament week, rates spike to $400–$700+ per night, and you're still 15–20 minutes from the course in heavy traffic.
  • Generic short-term rentals: Often shared properties, thin on amenities, and loaded with platform fees that add 15–20% to the sticker price.
  • Private waterfront properties: The sleeper category. Fewer of them exist, but they offer space, parking, and a way to actually decompress after a day on the grounds.

That third category is where KJ Augusta Rentals sits — and it's the reason this guide exists. More on that below.

Step 2: Understand Masters Tickets and the Practice Rounds

Masters badges are sold by lottery through Augusta National's official site, and the secondary market is expensive and legally gray. If you don't have badges, don't panic — the practice rounds (Monday through Wednesday) are easier to access and arguably more fun for first-timers. You can bring a camera on practice days (not during the tournament), players are more relaxed, and the Par 3 Contest on Wednesday is a genuine spectacle.

Practical ticket tips

  • Practice round tickets are significantly cheaper than tournament badges.
  • Gates typically open at 8 a.m.; arrive early to walk the course before crowds build.
  • Cell phones are prohibited on the grounds — plan your meetup points in advance.
  • Bring cash for the merchandise pavilion; the line moves faster than you'd expect.

Step 3: Master the Traffic and Parking Situation

This is where first-timers lose hours. Washington Road, Berckmans Road, and Alexander Drive all funnel into the same bottlenecks. The official free parking lots off Washington Road fill early, and rideshare surge pricing after the tournament ends is brutal.

The local trick is to stay somewhere with a back route. KJ Augusta Rentals sits on the Savannah River about 15 minutes from Augusta National via a private back route that avoids the Washington Road crawl entirely — a detail that sounds small until you've sat in tournament traffic at 6 p.m. with a sunburn and a cooler full of melting ice.

Traffic rules of thumb

  • Leave 90 minutes before your gate time, not 30.
  • Eastbound Washington Road is worse in the morning; westbound is worse after play.
  • If you're staying downtown, budget $40–$80 for event parking or use the shuttles.
  • If you're staying on the river, use the back roads and skip the strip entirely.

Step 4: Eat Like You Actually Live in Augusta

Downtown Augusta has a genuinely good food scene, and Masters Week is when it shines. A few standbys worth building your week around:

  • Broad Street: The heart of downtown dining. Farmhaus Burger, Craft & Vine, and the Bee's Knees are all within walking distance of the Riverwalk.
  • Surrey Center: A quieter, upscale cluster in Summerville with good brunch and coffee.
  • Local barbecue: Skip the chains. Augusta has real pitmasters if you ask around.
  • Groceries: If you're staying in a rental with a kitchen, stock up before Wednesday. Stores near the course get chaotic.

One underrated move: cook at your rental. After a long day walking 18 holes, a grilled dinner and a fire pit beat a two-hour restaurant wait every time.

Step 5: Build in Time Away From the Course

Masters Week is intense. The smartest visitors build in a rest day or two, and Augusta rewards it.

  • Augusta Riverwalk: A 2.5-mile paved trail along the Savannah River downtown — best at sunset.
  • Phinizy Swamp Nature Park: Quiet boardwalks and birding, 15 minutes from downtown.
  • Kayaking on the Savannah River: The stretch near the city is calm and scenic. If your lodging includes kayaks, use them.
  • Golf, obviously: There are public courses worth playing if you want to swing a club yourself.

This is another place where the right rental changes the trip. KJ Augusta Rentals includes six kayaks, a private dock, and a saltwater pool overlooking the river — so a rest day isn't a wasted day. It's the best day.

Where to Stay in Augusta for Masters Week

Here's the honest comparison most guides won't give you.

Downtown Augusta hotels

You get a bed and a lobby. During Masters Week you also get $500+ nightly rates, parking that costs extra or doesn't exist, no space to gather with your group, and a 20-minute drive to the course through the worst traffic of the year. If you're traveling solo or as a couple and just need a place to sleep, fine. If you're with a group, it's a compromise.

Generic short-term rentals

Shared properties, unclear guest policies, and platform fees that quietly add 15–20% to your total. You often don't know who else is on the property — which matters a lot when you're paying a premium for a once-a-year trip.

KJ Augusta Rentals

This is the category that actually fits Masters Week. KJ Augusta Rentals is a private 3-acre waterfront property directly on the Savannah River, sleeping up to 16 across 4 bedrooms — and crucially, there are no shared guests or other parties on site. You rent the entire property, or a smaller portion of it, and that's it.

What that looks like in practice:

  • Space to spread out: Fire pit, propane and charcoal grills, ping pong, cornhole, and a golf tee-off area — all on-site.
  • A saltwater pool overlooking the river: The single best way to recover after a day on your feet at Augusta National.
  • Six kayaks, a private dock, and a boat slip: Direct river access, no marina fees, no crowds.
  • A private back route to Augusta National: About 15 minutes, avoiding the Washington Road traffic that defines everyone else's week.

  • River Suite: Built for couples who want the waterfront without paying for space they won't use. See the river suite.

Check availability and book direct at kjaugustarentals.com — no platform fees, you pay the owner directly.

Step 6: Pack and Prep Like a Local

A few Masters Week specifics that catch visitors off guard:

  • No phones on the grounds. Bring a watch and agree on meetup spots.
  • Comfortable shoes matter more than anything else. Augusta National is hilly and you'll walk miles.
  • Sunscreen and a hat. April in Augusta is warm and the course has limited shade.
  • Book dining reservations weeks ahead if you want a sit-down dinner downtown.
  • Confirm your parking plan before you leave your lodging each morning.

The Bottom Line

Planning a Masters Week trip to Augusta comes down to three decisions: where you stay, how you handle traffic, and whether you build in time to actually enjoy the city. Get those right and it's a bucket-list week. Get them wrong and you'll spend it in a hotel parking garage.

The visitors who do it best stay somewhere with space, a back route, and a reason to come back to the property at the end of the day.
